MARKET.head: Bordeaux leads Liv-ex trade as Lynch-Bages 2005 becomes top-traded wine
MARKET.summ: US and UK buyers both upped their purchasing, the former segment reclaiming their share of purchasing
takeaways: Bordeaux held the lead with a 37.4% share of purchases on the Liv-ex trading platform this week.
Lynch-Bages 2005 was the region's top-traded wine, with Burgundy's share falling to 15.4% from 18.4%.
US buyers accounted for over half of Bordeaux's purchased value, rising to a 66.2% share of its traded value.

MARKET.head: Surrey backs 17 rural projects with £500,000 innovation grants
MARKET.summ: A wine producer using bird-repelling lasers and cattle farmer using GPS collars to track livestock are among 17 innovative projects funded from a £500,000 pot to boost Surrey’s rural economy. Surrey County Council’s Farming Innovation Accelerator supports farmers and growers with funding for projects to modernise operations,...
takeaways: Surrey County Council's Farming Innovation Accelerator funded 17 rural projects from a £500,000 pot of UK Shared Prosperity Funding.
Each recipient receives a grant of up to £35,000 plus bespoke expert support, drawn from more than 50 competitive proposals.
Albury Vineyard will install an automated bird-repellent laser to protect 18 acres of grapevines, adding over 1,700 bottles yearly.

MARKET.head: Navarra turns demanding rosé methods into a premium identity for its wines
MARKET.summ: How Navarra Rosado turned production challenges into premium positioning and a compelling marketing story. Andrea Ontiveros Flores, a sommelier and marketing & communications specialist from Alicante, Spain asks if English wine could do the same? Consumers rarely pay more simply because winemaking is difficult.
takeaways: Navarra rosado producers use the Saignée method, which can need up to three times more grapes than standard red production.
The Regulatory Council of D.O. Navarra introduced a Rosado Tradition designation requiring Saignée and exclusive Garnacha use.

MARKET.head: VinePair rounds up weekly beverage alcohol news and product releases
MARKET.summ: This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Heineken’s memo about effects of weight-loss drugs on drinking, RNDC’s Chapter 11 liquidation, and a ton of...
takeaways: A judge approved RNDC's Chapter 11 liquidation, according to VinePair's weekly roundup.
Heineken reportedly sent a memo on weight-loss drugs' effect on drinking, per the roundup's headlines.
Uncle Nearest's potential buyers are named as a headline item, with no further details given.

CULTURE.head: Volcanic soils give wines a distinctive tension, shaped by harsh vineyard conditions
CULTURE.summ:
Vines on volcanic soil are hard to grow and their grapes are hard-won, but it all combines to produce wines with a very particular sense of place

Good stories need jeopardy. Take The Princess Bride, one of my favourite films, which I recently introduced...
takeaways: Importer Nic Rizzi of Modal Wines says volcanic wines carry an extra tension that is hard to describe.
Volcanic soils including ash, basalt, obsidian, pumice and tuff vary widely, so the wines differ greatly in style.
Victoria Torres Pecis farms on La Palma in the Canaries, where a volcano erupted during harvest in 2021.

CULTURE.head: Plumpton College offers Level 3 Viticulture Apprenticeship for UK vineyards
CULTURE.summ: Develop the skills your business needs, invest in emerging talent and help shape the future of the UK wine industry with a Viticulture Apprenticeship at Plumpton College. As the UK wine industry continues to grow, developing a skilled workforce is essential to its long-term success. Plumpton College’s Level 3 Viticulture...
takeaways: Plumpton College is recruiting for its next Level 3 Viticulture Apprenticeship cohort, starting 9 November, with possible early-January joiners.
The apprenticeship is endorsed by WineGB and covers vineyard operative skills, with progression towards assistant vineyard manager.
Government funds 100% of training costs for eligible non-levy-paying SMEs' apprentices aged 16 to 24, subject to funding rules.

CULTURE.head: Real Housewives' wine tastes skew sweet, mass-market and status-driven, essayist argues
CULTURE.summ: What do the reality stars’ drinking habits reveal about wealth, taste, status and the economics of the U.S. wine industry?
takeaways: Cake Zine essayist, a certified wine specialist, watched Real Housewives franchises and noted their wine choices.
Housewives mostly drink mass-market, high-alcohol, sweet Californian cabernet sauvignon, such as Justin and Caymus.
The essay ties this sweet-wine preference to Robert Parker's 100-point system and the 'Parkerization' of flavour profiles.

SCIENCE.head: Pembrokeshire's Velfrey wins first Welsh trophy at Glass of Bubbly Awards
SCIENCE.summ: Pembrokeshire vineyard wins prestigious Glass of Bubbly trophy and gold medal, plus two silvers, competing against Champagne and sparkling wines from around the world A family-run vineyard in Pembrokeshire has
takeaways: Velfrey Vineyard, a family-run Pembrokeshire producer, won gold and the Winter Warmer Trophy at the Glass of Bubbly Awards 2026 for its Cuvée Reserve 2022.
It is the first Welsh wine ever to win a trophy at the competition, which judges Champagne and sparkling wines from around the world.
Its Rhosyn 2023 rosé and non-vintage Velfrey NV each took silver, giving the vineyard medals for all three wines entered.

SCIENCE.head: Enartis explains matching oak alternatives to specific winemaking goals
SCIENCE.summ: Oak remains one of the most powerful tools available to winemakers for shaping wine style, structure, and complexity. While traditional barrel ageing continues to play an important role, modern oak alternatives offer greater flexibility, lower cost, and increased precision when used with a clearly defined objective.
takeaways: Oak alternatives differ in surface area and toast level, which set how fast aromas release and which profile results.
Oak chips added during fermentation barely aid colour stability because oxygen is very low at that stage.
Colour stability gains come mainly during maturation when oak is combined with controlled oxygen, such as micro-oxygenation.

SCIENCE.head: English vines hit by 2026 heatwaves; Bacchus struggled, Sauvignon Blanc thrived
SCIENCE.summ: With harvest complete, or nearing completion on many vineyards, Hutchinsons agronomists Rob Saunders and Will Robinson look at the impact of the record-breaking summer and what we can learn for future seasons. While 2026 could be remembered as a vintage season for some growers, others will look back less fondly, having first...
takeaways: Fifty-four Met Office stations broke all-time daily maximum records this summer, peaking at 38.2°C in Gloucestershire in August.
Harvest ran 10-14 days earlier than normal, with Sauvignon Blanc showing high alcohol and phenolic ripeness while Bacchus struggled.
Viticulturist Markus Keller says heat stress starts above 30°C, with photosynthesis collapsing once leaf temperatures reach 40-45°C.

SCIENCE.head: UK vineyards navigate early, dry 2026 harvest driven by warmth and drought
SCIENCE.summ: After a run of dramatically different vintages, 2026 has given UK viticulture another season that challenged assumptions, but also demonstrated just how much English and Welsh vineyards can achieve. The 2026 growing season began with a series of extraordinary frost events, creating a challenging start before developing into a...
takeaways: The 2026 English and Welsh growing season began with severe frost events, then turned warm, dry and fast-ripening, with heat stress and water availability becoming key concerns.
Harvest arrived several weeks early at some UK vineyards, but dry weather kept disease pressure low and fruit arrived at wineries in excellent condition.
VineWorks argues UK growers can no longer plan around a typical season, so resilience needs building through soil health, water management, canopy control and variety choice.

SCIENCE.head: Domaine Bousquet details organic and water-saving practices at Mendoza winery
SCIENCE.summ: Domaine Bousquet continues to elevate Argentine wine through generations of dedication and innovation in organic wine practices. Earlier this year, Irma Remigio and her team warmly welcomed SWR’s Membership Manager, Ilva Fridenberga, to their winery. The winery, located at the foot of the Andes Mountains, is globally recognized...
takeaways: SWR Membership Manager Ilva Fridenberga visited Domaine Bousquet's Mendoza winery at the foot of the Andes in February.
The winery is trialling biodiversity and garden vineyard corridors, with harvest done from outside the vine rows.
It switched to high-pressure hoses for cleaning harvest boxes, using significantly less water, and is a signatory of the Bottle Weight Accord, targeting still bottles under 420g.

SCIENCE.head: MODIS satellite data used to map vineyard water use in Italy
SCIENCE.summ: In North-Eastern Italy water demand for vineyards irrigation is constantly increasing, but this conflicts with the high civil and industrial rates of water consumptions in the area, which is one of the most densely populated in Europe
takeaways: Researchers at the University of Padova used MODIS satellite data to estimate evapotranspiration in a 25-hectare northeastern Italian vineyard.
Estimates, combined with ground weather data, were calibrated on two years of eddy-covariance measurements and validated on two independent years.
Results showed good consistency with in situ observations, suggesting MODIS could monitor vineyard water use at regional scale.

SCIENCE.head: Grenache rootstocks and irrigation shape water use and stomatal control in Spain
SCIENCE.summ: Under the context of global change, any decrease in water use by crops is essential, because water is becoming a more and more scarce resource, especially in Mediterranean areas, where grapevines are grown
takeaways: IRTA researchers in Catalonia, Spain, grew three-year-old Grenache on rootstocks 110-R, 41-B and 161-49C, irrigated or non-irrigated.
Non-irrigated vines had higher water use efficiency, and 110-R and 41-B outperformed 161-49C.
Stomatal conductance differences from irrigation persisted through the season, suggesting hormonal signals outweighed hydraulic signals under these conditions.

SCIENCE.head: Italian researchers outline viticulture strategies for climate, water scarcity and biodiversity
SCIENCE.summ: In the globalization conditions possible future scenarios, optimistic and pessimistic are supposed
takeaways: Pisa University researchers outline future viticulture shaped by climate change, energy costs and genetic improvement.
They say Mediterranean water scarcity and native grape variety erosion require adaptable, resistant vine genotypes.
Their work studies Lazio varieties Malvasia and Cesanese d'Affile plus Cabernet Sauvignon under Cordon Spur of Conegliano training.

SCIENCE.head: Portuguese trial tests chemical and manual thinning to cut Vinhos Verdes vine yields
SCIENCE.summ: Some years, climate conditions and biological events increment the fertility of vines, which can lead to over cropping and a decrease of wine quality
takeaways: A 2007 trial in Vinhos Verdes compared Ethephon, Prohexadione-calcium and manual bunch thinning on Loureiro and Borraçal vines.
Manual bunch thinning cut Borraçal yield about 41% and Loureiro yield about 26% against the untreated control.
Ethephon significantly reduced crop, but only Loureiro showed quality gains, with higher sugar and lower acidity.

SCIENCE.head: Vine balance concept explained: growth, crop load and seasonal dynamics
SCIENCE.summ: Vine balance is a commonly used term in viticulture that expresses the concept of an appropriate balance of vegetative to reproductive growth of the vine
takeaways: Vine balance is the appropriate balance between a vine's vegetative growth and its reproductive growth, meaning fruit production.
Quantifying vine balance is hard, since most measures like yield to pruning weight ratio ignore seasonal growth dynamics.
A dynamic carbohydrate simulation model can show seasonal patterns of growth needs against canopy carbon supply.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Celebrating 25 years of Filipa Pato’s wines with an amazing lunch and tasting
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Flipa Pato, daughter of famous Bairrada winegrower Luis Pato, first started making her own wines 25 years ago, in 2001
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jamie Goode
takeaways: Filipa Pato, daughter of Luis Pato, began making her own wines in 2001 at age 25, now labelled with husband William Wouters.
Filipa and William farm 20 hectares across 37 plots, including the Missão vineyard, planted in 1864 and ungrafted.
Filipa uses pigs to regenerate soils and drone spraying for plant-derived treatments, though EU rules ban drone spraying of agrochemicals.

NEWSLETTERS.summ: The word you’re likely to hear most often while visiting the Douro wine region is schist. There’s a lot of
NEWSLETTERS.author: Alder Yarrow

NEWSLETTERS.head: Essential Kit for Kitchen Season
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Outfitting your kitchen with the season’s essential tools, plus this week’s favorite stories about food, wine, and culture
NEWSLETTERS.author: Meg Maker
takeaways: Meg Maker's Maker's Table piece frames November and December as "Kitchen Season," when cooking becomes a way to mark occasions.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Tasting Diaries: October 2026
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Niagara’s Cabernet Franc harvest finally gets underway, plus the bottles that made my October memorable
NEWSLETTERS.author: Cab Franc Chronicles
takeaways: Ontario's Niagara Peninsula saw unseasonably warm, dry October weather after one of its wettest summers on record, with Cabernet Franc harvest just starting, a little later than average.
Buttonwood Grove's 2025 Blanc de Franc from the Finger Lakes is a semi-sweet white Cabernet Franc with about 10 g/L residual sugar, priced at $24 USD.
Château de Fosse Sèche's 2018 Éolithe VDF from Saumur is described as fresh and elegant despite a very warm vintage, with at least five years of life ahead.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A New White Zin
NEWSLETTERS.summ: If you are not familiar with the lore of White Zinfandel , America’s greatest contribution to wine culture , you are missing out on some excellent cocktail conversation. I understand this might sound like the layup for a bad wine joke, but I’m not being facetious. White Zinfandel is as important to the United States
NEWSLETTERS.author: Tim Atkin MW
takeaways: Tim Atkin argues the US wine industry needs a 'new' White Zinfandel, as wine sales are at an all-time low.
Atkin proposes 'Relevé', a field blend of red and white grapes from an entire estate or region, inspired by Will Marengo's Feudal Project wine.

NEWSLETTERS.head: A deeper look at underwater wine aging
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Is a wine from the depths ‘better’ or does it depend on the boat?
NEWSLETTERS.author: Miquel Hudin
takeaways: Attis, a winery owned by Robustiano Fariña's family near O Grove, Galicia, ages its Albariño underwater in the local estuary.
The Attis Albariño 'Mar' is aged five months in 13-16C estuary waters, while the standard version produces about 120,000 bottles annually.
The author notes that underwater-aged wines he has tasted seemed tired and more advanced in age than landbound counterparts.

NEWSLETTERS.head: What to Know Before This Year’s Hospices de Beaune Wine Auction
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Discover the world's most famous charity wine auction held since 1859. Get essential tips and insights for this year's legendary Burgundy event
NEWSLETTERS.author: Jonathan Finch
takeaways: The 166th Hospices de Beaune wine auction is on Sunday 15 November 2026, with the 2026 vintage offered under the Halles de Beaune.
The 2026 crop is 432 barrels (348 red, 84 white), smaller than usual because an early heatwave reduced yields.
Last year's sale raised €18.8 million, with an average cask price of about €34,000 and Grand Crus averaging €86,290.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Visiting the Vineyard in the Sky
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The extraordinary story of Domaine de Beudon in Valais, Switzerland
NEWSLETTERS.author: Simon J. Woolf
takeaways: Domaine de Beudon, a Valais estate at 890 metres, is reachable only by a 90-minute hike or a cable car, with no road.
The Granges-Faiss family has farmed Beudon for over 50 years; Jacky bought it in 1971, and he died in June 2016 after a vineyard accident.
Marion Granges-Faiss has become the de facto winemaker, while the grapes ferment on the mountain but ageing and bottling happen at Pierre-Antoine Crettenand's Saillon winery.

NEWSLETTERS.head: Yet Another Vintage Port Flex Post (Tasting Selections From 1985 - 2022)
NEWSLETTERS.summ: Last week, I published a bunch of reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the (stellar) 2024 Port vintage. I typically follow those type of posts up with another post of other, older selections of vintage Ports that I tasted at the same event, and I offer them without much shame as simply […] This article was...
NEWSLETTERS.author: Joe Roberts
takeaways: 1WineDude published reviews from an NYC media tasting of selections from the 2024 Port vintage.
A follow-up post covers older vintage Ports from the same event, spanning 1985 to 2022.

NEWSLETTERS.head: 400 Montepulciano Bottles for Thomas Jefferson circa 1805
NEWSLETTERS.summ: The wine everyone’s been gushing over since the middle ages!
NEWSLETTERS.author: Eveline Chartier
takeaways: A 1350 trade contract between the Del Pecora family and merchant Jacopo di Vanni is the oldest known document for Vino Nobile di Montepulciano.
A 2024 document from the Jesuits of Montepulciano shows the term Vino Nobile was in use by 1766, earlier than the previously known 1787 record.
In 1806 Thomas Jefferson asked Thomas Appleton for 400 bottles of Montepulciano annually, sourced from ancient Jesuit vineyards.
